title: Jupiter: The Failed Star with a 300-Year-Old Hurricane
summary:
Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system — a gas giant so massive that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it. Some astronomers call it a failed star because it's made mostly of hydrogen and helium, the same elements that power stars.

If you tried to visit, you'd find no solid surface. Instead, you'd sink through clouds of ammonia and water vapor until the intense pressure and heat crushed you. Science fiction writers have proposed exploring Jupiter in hot-air balloons high above the crushing depths, but orbiting safely above is the smarter choice.

Jupiter's cloud bands race by at more than 300 miles per hour. Its most famous feature, the Great Red Spot, is a hurricane that has raged for centuries — and nearly three Earths could span it. Despite its size, Jupiter has the shortest day in the solar system: just 10 hours, thanks to its rapid rotation.

The planet also rules a system of nearly 70 moons. Ganymede is larger than Mercury and has its own magnetic field. Io is the most volcanic body in the solar system, spewing yellow sulfur clouds 300 miles high. And Europa, covered in ice, might hide a liquid ocean beneath its crust — an ocean that could contain life.

Jupiter generates radiation levels more than a thousand times the lethal dose, so any future explorers would need serious shielding. But for now, it's a spectacular place to study — a mini solar system all on its own.
why_it_matters: Jupiter is a natural laboratory for planetary science: its gravity shapes the architecture of the whole solar system, and its icy moons may be among the most reachable places to look for life beyond Earth. At the same time, its extreme radiation and storms set hard engineering limits on future exploration, and studying a 'failed star' sharpens our understanding of what actually separates a planet from a star.

background_read: Jupiter is a gas giant — a planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface — and it is the largest planet in the solar system. Stars also run on hydrogen, which is why Jupiter earns the nickname 'failed star'. The real difference is mass: a ball of hydrogen has to be roughly eighty times heavier than Jupiter for its core to ignite nuclear fusion and shine.

In 1610 the astronomer Galileo Galilei (an Italian scientist whose telescope observations reshaped astronomy) pointed a homemade telescope at Jupiter and found four large moons circling it — the first hard evidence that not everything in the sky orbits the Earth. Those moons are still called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

NASA's Juno spacecraft (launched in 2011 and orbiting Jupiter since 2016) has been measuring the planet's gravity, magnetic field and storms, adding detail to what flyby missions like Pioneer and Voyager first revealed. Jupiter's magnetic field is enormously stronger than Earth's, which is one reason its radiation belts are so dangerous.

Europa is considered one of the best places to search for life beyond Earth because a salty ocean may lie beneath its ice. A NASA mission called Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, is designed to study that moon up close in the 2030s, while the European Space Agency's JUICE spacecraft is on a similar journey.

perspectives.description: Jupiter offers several scientific prizes at once: a window into how giant planets and their moon systems form, and icy moons like Europa that may hold habitable oceans. Missions such as Juno, Europa Clipper and JUICE turn the Jovian system into the most intensively studied planetary neighborhood after Mars.

Exploring Jupiter is brutally expensive and technically punishing: any spacecraft near the planet needs radiation hardening, and the intense belts and crushing pressures rule out easy direct sampling. The 'failed star' label is catchy but can mislead people into thinking Jupiter is nearly a star, when it is nowhere close in mass.

Galileo's discovery of four moons orbiting Jupiter in 1610 helped dethrone the idea that everything circles the Earth, making Jupiter central to the birth of modern astronomy. Four centuries later, the same system is again the testbed for a new question — whether life can exist in oceans sealed under ice, far from sunlight.

Europa Clipper and JUICE are set to arrive in the 2030s and will try to confirm whether Europa's subsurface ocean is real and potentially habitable. If it is, attention may shift toward designing a lander, which would face the hardest radiation environment any mission has attempted.
